data.title: Meet the next generation of Chinese stars making their mark in global finance
data.description:
A new generation of Chinese stars is influencing how global finance operates – applying analytical power, cross-cultural agility, and resilience developed in China’s demanding environments straight to leading firms from Citadel Securities to BlackRock.
That shift is easier to grasp by looking beyond the Ivy League feeder pipelines to the mathematical boot camps of Shenzhen and the lecture halls of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.
The careers of these figures – Tian Zhou, Wei Li, Katherine Wu and Han Jiarui – exemplify how Chinese talent has climbed into senior roles across hedge funds, asset management, and crypto.
Tian Zhou: regional prodigy who became partner at 30
In July 2026, eFinancialCareers listed the top 13 London hedge fund partners under 35, based on data from Companies House, the UK agency that maintains the register of companies. Tian Zhou’s name and age stood out.
Zhou’s story began far from the prestigious halls of the US Ivy League universities. He started at Guangxi University, a regional school in southern China, throwing himself into electrical engineering and English with the intense discipline that would define his career.
That grit powered his transfer to Central Michigan University, where he double-majored in electrical engineering and mathematics, graduating with a perfect 4.0 grade point average and summa cum laude honors.
He then earned a master’s degree with distinction from University College London (UCL), according to his LinkedIn profile.
He joined Citadel after graduating from UCL in 2019 and became a partner and associate portfolio manager by age 30, according to eFinancialCareers.
Becoming a partner at Citadel is one of the most exclusive achievements in the hedge fund industry.
Zhou has become a major inspiration for mainland Chinese students and parents, showing that perpetual academic rigor can take you from a regional Chinese university to the heights of global finance.
Wei Li: an inspiration beyond markets
Before Wei Li became global chief investment strategist at the BlackRock Investment Institute, she was a maths prodigy in Shenzhen’s competitive school system.
A two-time Mathematical Olympiad gold medallist in China, her analytical precision prowess enabled her to attend Cambridge University and, eventually, jobs at Lehman Brothers and Citigroup.
Her journey from Shenzhen’s classroom competitions to Bloomberg and CNBC screens shows how Chinese mathematical discipline helps shape the global investment narrative.
Her influence extends beyond global markets, resonating deeply with parents and young women in China who see in her an inspiring combination of intellect, poise, global fluency and professional authority.
On RedNote (known as Xiaohongshu in China), the online community often describes her with a phrase that has become emblematic: “Beauty is the least noteworthy of her strengths.”
Katherine Wu: bridge to future finance
Katherine Wu’s influence in Web3 is defined by her ability to bridge worlds. Born in California but raised across Kunming, the capital of China’s southwestern Yunnan province, Hong Kong, and the US, she graduated from Johns Hopkins University, earned a law degree at the Cardozo School of Law in New York, but pivoted early into crypto.
She worked as a key operator at Messari, a principal at Notation Capital, and senior lead at Coinbase Ventures, where she expanded the team and oversaw a record year of early-stage investments in 2021.
“2021 was a record year for Coinbase Ventures, with just under 150 deals, averaging a new deal every 2.5 days. On a cumulative basis, more than 90 per cent of the capital Coinbase Ventures deployed since inception [was invested that year].” noted in the Coinbase newsletter, Around the Block.
While many crypto funds focus solely on the investment process, Wu’s background also allowed her to provide additional value by offering strategic, legal and operational guidance to portfolio companies.
Now a Venture Partner at Archetype and chief operating officer of ENS Labs, she continues to shape the future of the blockchain ecosystem via her multi-disciplinary background.
Han Jiarui: homecoming quant titan
Han Jiarui’s professional journey is a masterclass in bringing Wall Street excellence back to China. With a PhD in statistics from Stanford University in California, he served as head of Asia quant research at Citadel, with a prior role at Two Sigma.
After honing his expertise at these top firms, Han recognised that combining Western experience with a deep understanding of the Chinese market was a potent mix.
He returned home and in 2021 founded Shenzhen-based ZenX Quant, where he tripled assets under management to US$2 billion in under six months, according to a Bloomberg report in May.
ZenX started strong. Its index-enhancement strategies all beat their benchmarks in the first year, delivering average excess returns of more than 3 per cent.
Its CSI A500 tracker outpaced the index by 25.6 per cent between the end of 2024 and February 27.
Most striking, one strategy benchmarked to the small-cap CSI 2000 has generated an excess return of 153 per cent since 2023, according to information provided by Bloomberg.
Partnering with Citic Securities, ZenX tapped into China’s massive distribution channels. Han’s rise mirrors a broader gold rush in China’s asset management industry.
The country’s private securities investment funds surpassed 8 trillion yuan (US$1.2 trillion) in assets under management for the first time at the end of June, emerging as the core engine driving the expansion of the country’s private fund industry, according to data from the Asset Management Association of China in July.

data.title: Parents urged to vaccinate children amid flu, Covid-19 and RSV infection cases
data.description:
Hong Kong parents should have their children vaccinated against respiratory infections as the city faces a triple threat from influenza, Covid-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a medical expert has said.
Dr Mike Kwan Yat-wah, an honorary clinical associate professor in the University of Hong Kong’s department of paediatrics and adolescent medicine, warned on Saturday that the current summer flu season had yet to reach its peak. His remarks came four days after the city recorded its first child death from flu this year.
“The number [of flu cases] remains high and there is no sign of it dropping yet, therefore it is unclear when the peak will arrive,” he said.
Covid-19 and RSV cases were also at high levels, Kwan said, warning that Hong Kong was under threat from three types of infections.
“We are now under the triple attack of flu, Covid-19 and RSV … this triple whammy is happening in Hong Kong and neighbouring areas,” he said.
He urged parents to have their children vaccinated if they had not already done so.
Kwan said children could still be protected by receiving flu jabs for the 2025-26 season, before receiving vaccines for the 2026-27 season under the government’s vaccination scheme.
“Parents need not hesitate … Vaccines for [these two seasons] are different. There is also no need to space them apart for a specific period of time,” he said.
Covid-19 vaccine supplies for young children have been temporarily suspended because the jabs have expired. But Kwan said other vulnerable groups, including elderly people, chronically ill patients and those who had caught the virus more than six months earlier, should still get inoculated.
According to the latest data from the Centre for Health Protection, influenza activity in Hong Kong remained high after the summer flu season began on July 2.
Of respiratory specimens handled by the public laboratory in the week ending August 1, 9.94 per cent tested positive for flu, slightly lower than the 10.65 per cent recorded the previous week.
Twenty flu outbreaks were recorded in various institutions last week, mostly in care homes for the elderly.
Covid-19 activity also remained elevated, according to the centre’s data. Infections began rising in June, with the public laboratory detecting 700 new cases in the week from July 26 to August 1.

Eighteen Covid-19 outbreaks were reported in homes for elderly and disabled people over the same period.
The laboratory has also recorded a rise in RSV infections since late June, when the number of detected cases exceeded 200, compared with a few dozen during the non-peak period.
The number peaked at 323 in the second last week of July before falling slightly to 265 last week.
On Tuesday, the city reported its first fatal paediatric flu case of the year, involving a seven-year-old boy who had contracted influenza A (H3). The boy, who had been in good health and vaccinated, first developed symptoms on July 27.
“I hope this serious case does not undermine public confidence in vaccines. It is an isolated case,” Kwan said.
Without commenting on the specific case, Kwan said some people’s immunity might weaken several months after vaccination. The city’s 2025-26 vaccination scheme began in September last year.
He added that some people might be born with weaker immunity because of genetic predispositions.
Kwan said experts might also need to analyse whether the currently circulating H3 strain had undergone genetic changes that could cause more severe reactions in patients.
The Department of Health said on Wednesday that the government had procured 1.3 million doses of flu vaccines for the 2026-27 season.
About 530,000 doses of inactivated vaccine from Sinovac will arrive in Hong Kong from later this month. Another batch of around 660,000 doses of inactivated vaccine from Sanofi will be delivered from mid-October.
The remaining supplies include about 60,000 doses of nasal spray vaccine from AstraZeneca and another 60,000 doses of recombinant vaccine from Sanofi.
The government has also announced that Covid-19 jabs offered to people aged 12 or above under its vaccination programme will be temporarily suspended after September 5, when the current batch expires. Supplies for children aged six months or above were suspended earlier.
Covid-19 vaccination services under the government programme will resume in the fourth quarter of this year.

data.title: ‘Addiction is irreversible’: Hong Kong urged to ban under-16s from social media
data.description:
Hong Kong should follow international peers in legislating to bar children under 16 from social media to combat cyberbullying and addiction, education experts and lawmakers have said, while stressing the need for broad social consensus.
At a panel discussion on Saturday to examine proposals to restrict social media access for under-16s, educators and lawmakers argued that legislation was needed to signal the government’s stance and drive efforts to prevent the next generation from being harmed by such platforms.
Lilian Chan Lui Ling-yee, honorary president of the Yan Oi Association of Principals and a seasoned educator, said social media addiction was the biggest problem facing education and that legislation was required to protect children.
“Some say that whether we ban it or not, children will still face the same environment, but I do not agree. If we do not legislate, the future of our next generation will be lost,” Chan, who has served as principal at different schools, said.
“Social media addiction is irreversible – you lose your judgement, like losing a compass at sea. Legislation will raise public awareness about protecting children from harmful content on social media, such as pornography and cyberbullying.”
A survey by the policy group New Youth Forum interviewed 686 randomly selected residents aged 18 or above between May 22 and June 5. It found 61.8 per cent of respondents backed legislation restricting under-16s from social media, with support rising to 76.3 per cent among parents.

But the poll also revealed a sharp generational divide: 51.7 per cent of 18- to 29-year-olds opposed the move, while older age groups were far more supportive.
Tang Wing-chun, convenor of the New Youth Forum, said enacting such a law would be a lengthy process requiring greater engagement with young people and more education for parents and children on social media use to foster broader social discussion.
Lawmaker Duncan Chiu said Hong Kong’s commitment to information freedom made it difficult to follow the mainland’s model of erecting firewalls and establishing a central online supervision body, but policymakers and the education sector could help identify implementation areas and loopholes at the execution level.
“In some European countries phones are banned on campuses and access to social media is restricted, so I think execution would most likely start with schools first, and then we will see how to push that back to the home,” he said.
“We should be aware that children are now smart enough to find ways to evade supervision – even now internet cafes are becoming more popular as a way to evade parent and school control.”
France has enforced a nationwide mobile phone ban for students up to middle school since 2018, with many schools requiring devices to be kept in pouches or lockers during the day. Authorities are extending the prohibition to senior secondary schools from the 2026-27 academic year.
In Britain, a statutory ban on smartphones in state-funded schools across England took effect on June 29, requiring pupils to switch off or store their devices throughout the school day.
Former prime minister Keir Starmer also unveiled plans in June to bar all children under 16 from social media, adopting the same model as Australia, which in December 2025 became the first country in the world to impose such age restrictions.

data.title: Hong Kong commerce chief to lead joint local and mainland delegation to Malaysia
data.description:
Hong Kong’s commerce chief is set to lead a delegation of mainland Chinese and local firms to Malaysia next week, noting that about 200 enterprises from across the border have already set up offices in the city since last year, using it as a stepping stone to go global.
Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah also said on Saturday that the city was eyeing emerging markets in Africa, after exploring the Middle East and Central Asia amid geopolitical tensions.
Yau said the coming Malaysia trip would involve exploring business opportunities and signing agreements to confirm bilateral investments.
“The trip is not just to help mainland and Hong Kong enterprises go overseas, but also to potentially attract businesses from other places to Hong Kong … which could help develop the city’s economy,” the minister said.
“This could also in turn help strengthen the industry chain, which could support boosting mainland China’s domestic circulation.”
“Domestic circulation” refers to China’s economic strategy of self-reliance by creating a robust domestic market.
Since the establishment of the GoGlobal Task Force last October, about 200 mainland enterprises have set up in Hong Kong and are using the city as a stepping stone for their overseas expansion plans, according to Yau.
“Hong Kong is experienced in global business whereas many mainland enterprises are yet to fully grasp the culture, legal system, and trade overseas,” he said.
“We encourage them to set up regional headquarters or offices here, which would be good for Hong Kong’s economy.”
He elaborated by saying that would mean renting and hiring in Hong Kong, and using the professional services – such as law, accounting, and authentication – the city offers, as well as fundraising and financing before going international.
Thousands of enterprises had taken part in the forums the task force hosted in Beijing, Shanghai and Shandong, with the chief executive bringing a delegation of Hong Kong and mainland businesses to Central Asia earlier this year, Yau said.
In promoting Hong Kong trade, the minister said it was important to maintain strong ties with long-term partners such as the European, American and Asean markets while exploring the Middle Eastern, Central Asia and Latin American markets, and beyond.
“Turkey is an important Eurasian platform while Egypt is the gateway to Africa. We hope to visit these two countries,” he said.
Yau also said on Saturday he was certain the city was on track to exceed the government’s target for attracting foreign investment, after more than 400 enterprises set up offices in Hong Kong in the first half of the year, bringing in over HK$50 billion (US$6.4 billion) in capital.

InvestHK, the government’s investment arm, has been tasked with attracting at least 1,200 mainland Chinese or overseas enterprises to establish or expand in Hong Kong between 2026 and 2027, bringing in direct investment of no less than HK$120 billion.
“I am very confident that they will exceed the target,” Yau said.
While he said the introduction of enterprises would create job opportunities in the city with “many sectors hiring”, he also called on young people to equip themselves and explore where such opportunities were, especially amid the rise of artificial intelligence (AI).
“The global economy is changing, especially with the advent of AI, which is causing many companies’ business models to shift, particularly the digital economy and e-commerce,” he said.
“Young people will need to think in line with global trends for their employment.”

data.title: Temperatures exceed 38 degrees as Severe Typhoon Dolphin brings extreme heat
data.description:
Temperatures exceeded 38 degrees Celsius (100 Fahrenheit) in parts of Hong Kong on Saturday as the city’s forecaster warned that extremely hot weather would persist over the coming days.
The Hong Kong Observatory said Severe Typhoon Dolphin was bringing high temperatures to the region, with the heat expected to continue into early next week.
“With [Severe Typhoon] Dolphin moving towards the vicinity of Zhejiang and northern Fujian, its outer subsiding air will persistently bring extremely hot weather to the area in the next couple of days,” the Observatory said.
A very hot weather warning was issued at 6.45am, while the Labour Department issued an amber heat stress at work warning about 15 minutes later.
The temperature reached 34.1 degrees at the Observatory’s headquarters in Tsim Sha Tsui at around 1.30pm. Elsewhere, temperatures climbed well above 35 degrees in the afternoon.
Sheung Shui recorded the city’s highest temperature, reaching 38.5 degrees shortly before 2pm. Temperatures of 37.1 degrees were also recorded in Yuen Long Park and at The Peak.
The Observatory urged residents to drink plenty of water and take all necessary precautions to protect themselves from the heat.
“Avoid vigorous outdoor physical activities,” it said. “If symptoms such as dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion develop, rest and seek help immediately, and seek medical advice as soon as possible.”
The forecaster said the extremely hot weather would persist over the coming days, with temperatures in parts of the city forecast to reach or exceed 37 degrees.
Sunday is expected to be mainly fine, with extreme heat during the day and a possibility of isolated showers.

data.title: ‘Path open’ for revival of CUHK student union – if it registers, Dennis Lo says
data.description:
The president of the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has said “the path is open” for the revival of the institution’s main student union, so long as it registers with authorities in accordance with the law.
Dennis Lo Yuk-ming also pushed back on claims that the university was overreliant on intake from mainland China, arguing that it was making strides in diversification.
In an interview with the South China Morning Post, he said the pathway to re-establishing a central union remained available through legal registration, pointing to the two college unions that had already done so, but offered no timetable.
“Our position has never changed. The student union will need to go through Hong Kong’s legal procedures. We require registration under the Societies Ordinance or the Companies Ordinance,” Lo said.
“Among our nine colleges, SH Ho College and Morningside College have already done so – this proves the path is open. We have colleagues actively in touch with students to help them through this process.”
In March 2021, the main student union’s cabinet, known as “Syzygia”, resigned after CUHK warned that the organisation faced legal risks under the national security law. The university also cut off the group’s fee collection capabilities and administrative support.
The union formally announced its dissolution in October of that year.
The University of Hong Kong’s student union also disbanded in August 2021, with groups at Baptist University and Polytechnic University, among other campuses, following suit after demands that they undergo independent registration.
On Thursday evening, Lingnan University’s student union announced its dissolution as well. The move leaves the union at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology as the only one still operating on campus among the city’s publicly funded universities.
City University’s student union also remains active, but has been operating out of a space in Cheung Sha Wan after the institution cut ties with it and ordered it to vacate campus premises in 2022.
CUHK’s student union was a federal union of nine college affiliates that supplied its membership and electoral mandate.

The central union was first notified of the need to register in February 2021, before the requirement was extended to constituent college unions in 2023, because they maintained independent finances and electoral systems – meaning they risked being deemed illegal unless they registered.
Between January 2024 and January 2026, seven college unions ceased operations after their respective colleges withdrew recognition, with student leaders citing risks to their autonomy.
While the central union has ceased to function, other student bodies representing specific populations continue to operate independently, including the Mainland Undergraduate Association and the International Student Association.
Asked whether a revived union framework should incorporate greater diversity to reflect the campus’s increasingly mixed student body, Lo said the university and its colleges continued to provide support for student activities, with participation numbers growing.
“Some of our colleges have many non-local students. Morningside College, for example, is a model for internationalisation. It is one of their traditions,” he said. “We will definitely make our university more international, more diverse, more inclusive.”
The government earlier doubled the non-local student quota for publicly funded universities to the equivalent of 40 per cent of local places, starting from the 2024-25 academic year, before the threshold was raised to 50 per cent from 2026-27 under last year’s policy address.
At CUHK, non-local undergraduates accounted for about 24 per cent of the student body in 2025-26, up from 17.3 per cent the previous year.
Official figures showed that 71 per cent of the university’s non-local undergraduate students in 2025-26 were from the mainland.

Pushing back against claims of an overreliance on mainland students, Lo noted that the university was attracting more applications from international candidates.
“Looking at the statistics, non-local applications have increased by 20 per cent year on year. But if you break it down, out-of-China applications have actually increased by 75 per cent. So I believe we are already seeing some results in diversification,” Lo said.
With student numbers set to grow under the expanded quota, he said the university would need to recruit more academics, adding that 56 per cent of CUHK professors were already non-locals.
“We are grateful for the government’s schemes, including the Frontier Technology Research Support Scheme, which provide matching funds to recruit talent,” he said.
“These professors will need laboratories. That is why we have Area 39, where a new medical school building is now under construction, and why we will conduct a campus master plan exercise to map out new facilities over the next decade. We hope to build more to attract more staff.”
CUHK unveiled its five-year strategic plan on Thursday, with major development slated for Area 39. The plan includes establishing a postgraduate college, which will extend the university’s collegiate system to master’s and PhD students.
Asked whether local scholars were being displaced by the growing non-local faculty ranks, Lo, who began his career at CUHK in 1997, said the academic job market and research funding had expanded rapidly over the past three decades.
“The posts were much fewer then, and the research grants were much smaller,” he said. “If you hired a postdoc for two years, it would basically eat up your entire grant.”
He noted that the research funding pool was now so much larger that the total number of positions had risen alongside the influx of international hires.
“I think it is much more exciting now to be a scholar in Hong Kong compared with my time,” he said.

data.title: Man found with knife wounds before another falls to death at same Hong Kong block
data.description:
Hong Kong police are investigating after a man with multiple knife wounds was found in a lift at a public housing block in Wong Tai Sin, seven minutes before another man was discovered to have fallen to his death at the same building.
Police received the first report at 7.19am on Saturday after the injured man was found inside a lift at Chiu Sin House in Upper Wong Tai Sin Estate.
The man, who had sustained several knife wounds, was taken to Queen Elizabeth Hospital for treatment. Police said he had been found by a building security guard.
At 7.26am, police received another report that a man had fallen from a height at the same building. He landed on a platform in the housing estate and was certified dead at the scene.
The force did not confirm whether the two men knew each other or whether the incidents were connected, saying the cases had not officially been combined.
The first case was classified as wounding and referred to the Wong Tai Sin district crime squad. The second was classified as suicide.
If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline.
You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services.
In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

data.title: Bar Association broadly backs new offence for persistent child sexual abuse
data.description:
The Hong Kong Bar Association has said it “broadly supports” a dedicated offence for persistent child sexual abuse, after concerns over evidential issues in such cases were resolved in other jurisdictions in the past two decades.
Vice-chairman Martin Hui Siu-ting said that while the association had reversed previous reservations it expressed when the city last discussed such a proposal in 2001, the new offence would require safeguards to ensure both sides were treated fairly at trial.
“We broadly agree to the introduction of such an offence of persistent child sexual abuse, which somehow reflects the past experience of at least 20 years of different jurisdictions within the criminal system,” Hui said.
While the government’s proposed overhaul of outdated sexual offence laws does not include provisions for a dedicated offence for persistent child sexual abuse, assault survivors and advocates have called for discussions on the issue to be reopened to plug loopholes.
With a one-month consultation period on the proposals having ended, Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that his bureau would “actively consider” calls to introduce a separate offence for persistent child sexual abuse.
Authorities previously attempted to introduce such an offence between 2001 and 2002 to allow prosecutors to lay charges for long-term, repetitive sexual abuse even when the child concerned could not accurately recall the exact circumstances of each incident.
The proposal arose following a 1999 ruling by the Court of Final Appeal, which quashed the convictions of a man accused of repeatedly sexually assaulting his stepdaughter when she was nine after rejecting the “at least once” approach to prosecution.
Under the previous proposal, prosecutors could lay the charge by proving that abuse had been committed against a child on at least three occasions on different days, but without having to specify or prove the exact circumstances of each alleged offence.
The association, the professional regulatory body for barristers, and the Hong Kong Law Society, which regulates solicitors, made a joint submission opposing the proposal at the time. They said it would not be possible to specify a representative number of charges, while defendants might not have a clear idea of the allegations against them.
Hui, a criminal law specialist, said legal developments in other common law jurisdictions since the city’s previous discussions and the 1999 ruling had overcome difficulties in raising evidence, as well as those relating to the burden and standard of proof in such cases.
Hui said that after studying similar offences in Australia’s six states and two territories, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, Canada and South Africa, the association now supported the city establishing an offence for cases in which individual charges covering events that took place over a long period would not be possible.
“I share such a concern as well, that a child who suffered persistent sexual abuse over a long period of time may perceive trauma as an undifferentiated whole rather than as separate events,” Hui said.
The senior counsel proposed four “safeguards” to ensure fairness for both the defendant and the victim, as well as the integrity of court rulings.
He said the first was that prosecutors should consider the use of individual substantive charges first, if possible, rather than relying on the new offence.




Prosecutors should also not be allowed to charge a defendant with both persistent child sexual abuse and other substantive sexual offences, such as rape, at the same time, or to amend a substantive sexual offence charge to the persistent sexual abuse charge at the end of submitting evidence in a trial.
“Ideally, we suggest that it should be made clear that there are two forms of offending. For instance, a substantive charge of rape, and on the other hand, a persistent sexual abuse offence,” Hui said.
“These offences are legally distinct and cannot be treated as alternatives to each other.”
He added that the association would also suggest requiring the consent of the secretary for justice before prosecutions under the offence could be launched.
Hui stressed that the safeguards would not make the persistent child sexual abuse offence a last resort for prosecutors, but would maintain procedural and legal integrity.
“These safeguards are to ensure that if we have this new offence, it would operate fairly and impartially and the court would know the imperatives of the balanced interest of both the complainants and the defendants in a trial,” Hui said.
On the proposed reforms, Hui said that a non-exhaustive list of 11 scenarios that would not constitute consent to a sexual act should remain open to dispute at trial to protect defendants’ rights.
“If there is evidence raised that the complainant did in fact consent, it should remain open to the court, the tribunal of fact, or the jury to consider that evidence in assessing whether lack of consent is proven,” Hui said.
The veteran barrister added that while the proposed reforms were a “major leap forward” in modernising the law, as many offences dated back decades and had roots in English law in the 1950s, authorities had to keep abreast of technology and victims’ conditions to ensure adequate protection.
“There must also, we suggest, be a nuanced understanding of the plight of the victims of such sexual abuse to better understand how the law can best protect these victims going forward,” Hui said.

data.title: CUHK chief urges more funds for campuses in Northern Metropolis university town
data.description:
The leader of the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has called for greater financial support to develop a proposed 300-hectare (741 acres) university town near the border with mainland China, including funding for local institutions to build campuses, arguing that expansion will help navigate future challenges.
In a wide-ranging interview with the South China Morning Post, CUHK president Dennis Lo Yuk-ming said Hong Kong universities needed to expand their presence in the Northern Metropolis university town, where institutions could gain significant advantages and make a greater impact.
Lo, a globally renowned scientist and molecular geneticist who studied at two leading UK universities, Oxford and Cambridge, said Hong Kong institutions’ main weakness was their small size and limited scale.
“If we compare ourselves to international competitors, our weakness is size and scale, as city university campuses are relatively small. Our universities are like boutique hotels,” he said, explaining that the institutions were excellent but had limited capacity.
He added that world university rankings were constrained by institutional size, a factor considered by some ranking agencies.
“Some well-known universities on the mainland have multiple campuses, but Hong Kong has had no such luxury until now. The Northern Metropolis offers a valuable opportunity for us to expand, especially given that land in Hong Kong is such a precious resource,” he said.
Under the Northern Metropolis megaproject, 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land near the border with Shenzhen will be transformed into a hub that includes innovation and technology business parks, housing estates and the university town.
Lo urged Hong Kong universities to remain alert to future challenges, stressing that the sector needed to scale up by expanding into the mega-development.
The proposed university town is expected to be a key feature of the city’s first five-year blueprint.
The town will include 300 hectares of core campus areas spanning Hung Shui Kiu, Ngau Tam Mei and New Territories North. Land will be developed in phases, with the first tender set to be launched next month and the first plot expected to be formed by the end of this year.
Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin said last month that a HK$10 billion (US$1.2 billion) loan scheme earmarked to support campus development would apply only to Hung Shui Kiu, which covers just 22 hectares.

Lo said funding was one of the critical factors in planning the town, as its overall size was more than twice that of CUHK’s current campus.
“What I want to know most about the town is the funding arrangement … mainland governments fully subsidise the cost of building mainland university campuses. I wonder whether the Hong Kong government will strengthen its financial support for developing this town,” he said.
The government has repeatedly said the town will be self-financing, with support offered through low-interest loan schemes with longer repayment periods.
Lo argued that construction costs in Hong Kong were high and that the government’s HK$10 billion committed for loans was insufficient. He added that universities were eager to discuss funding arrangements further with officials.
“Our new medical building, which is currently under construction, costs over HK$3 billion. We in Hong Kong have ambition and we have land; the next thing we need is the resources to make these dreams come true,” he said.




He added that he understood the city’s public finances had come under enormous pressure two years earlier, and that institutions at the time had been willing to share the financial burden with the government.
Asked how much of a commitment the government should make, Lo said it should be a “big number” invested over several years, rather than a one-off commitment.
Regarding overseas university-town models worth considering, Lo said there was no need for the city to copy others, as Hong Kong was unique.
“Hong Kong is so unique that there is no other place we can simply copy and paste. That is what makes us special. No other city of our size possesses such high international standing, boasts five Top 100 universities, and enjoys the backing of a vast hinterland in the Greater Bay Area,” he said.
CUHK rose to 18th in the QS world university rankings this year, its highest-ever position.

Lo said rankings were only one of many ways to evaluate a university, akin to a health check, and were by no means the sole metric.
“All ranking results are encouraging to us, built on the efforts of generations at CUHK over 60 years. None of this could be achieved overnight,” he said.
However, QS’s Best Student Cities rankings suggested that Hong Kong’s high tuition fees, compared with elsewhere in East Asia, could deter international students.
CUHK’s tuition fee for non-local undergraduate students for the 2026-27 academic year is HK$214,000.
The rankings placed Hong Kong 17th among the world’s top destinations for international students.
Lo defended tuition fee levels for international students in Hong Kong, arguing that they were not excessively high.
“Some of our competitors in the United States are much more expensive as some of their fees are double Hong Kong’s level,” he said.
“With the non-local student quota increased to 50 per cent, accommodating them incurs costs, such as hiring more professors. A fee of around HK$200,000 per year is not that expensive.”
Addressing the shortage of hostel places across local universities, Lo noted that CUHK had already guaranteed non-local undergraduates two years of campus accommodation.

data.title: Cambricon posts 108% surge in revenue amid China’s massive AI chip drive
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant Cambricon Technologies reported a 108 per cent surge in first-half revenue on Friday, as the firm capitalises on a massive domestic push to replace foreign AI hardware.
The chipmaker’s revenue for the first six months of the year reached 6 billion yuan (US$890 million), while profits also jumped 122.6 per cent year on year to 2.3 billion yuan, according to a stock exchange filing.
In the second quarter, the firm’s revenue was 3.1 billion yuan, in line with the consensus estimate of 3 billion yuan predicted by a Bloomberg poll. Net profit reached 1.3 billion yuan, up from 1 billion yuan during the previous quarter.
The company attributed the revenue surge to a steady increase in demand for AI computing power during the first six months. “Leveraging our core competitiveness in AI chips, we continued to strengthen in-depth cooperation with leading enterprises in the finance and internet sectors,” it said in the filing.
The earnings jump underscores the broader boom in China’s AI chip sector, fuelled by Beijing’s sweeping push for tech self-sufficiency as well as a monumental AI infrastructure buildout across the nation.
With US export controls largely cutting off China’s access to advanced AI accelerators from companies like Nvidia, domestic designers are rushing to fill the market vacuum.


Cambricon’s Shanghai-listed stock closed up 2.7 per cent at nearly 1,200 yuan ahead of the earnings release on Friday. The company was the most valuable stock on Shanghai’s tech-focused STAR market until July, when it was overtaken by memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) following its blockbuster market debut.
Cambricon has previously outlined ambitious plans to dramatically scale its operations.
In July, the company set a target of generating more than 100 billion yuan in revenue over the three years to 2028 – a nearly 20-fold increase from its previous plan set three years earlier, which aimed for 4.6 billion yuan of cumulative revenue between 2024 and 2026. The higher target was set as part of the firm’s roll-out of a new staff stock incentive plan.
The momentum lifting Cambricon is also rippling across the rest of the domestic AI chip sector.
Beijing-based Moore Threads expected its first-half revenue to rise up to 149 per cent year on year to 1.75 billion yuan, citing strong demand for its MTT S5000 graphics processing unit and rapid commercialisation of its intelligent computing clusters.
Hygon Information Technology, another leader in the domestic AI processor sector, forecast first-half revenue of up to 9.3 billion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 70 per cent.
Still, analysts expect Cambricon to face mounting challenges amid fierce domestic competition.
“Competition is likely to intensify as peers launch new products in second half of 2026, testing Cambricon’s relative performance and price-to-performance positioning,” Morgan Stanley analysts said in a research note last week.
In the filing, Cambricon said it was developing a next-generation intelligent processor microarchitecture and instruction set – though it did not disclose a launch date – as well as optimising systems on the software side.

data.title: Hong Kong designer sues Prada for US$5m over abandoned Rolls-Royce project
data.description:
A Hong Kong-based Belgian designer is taking fashion powerhouse Prada to court, claiming at least US$5 million in damages for the alleged repudiation of a partnership agreement to redesign a series of Rolls-Royce cars for exhibitions and events worldwide.
In a High Court lawsuit filed on Thursday, Jonathan Riss accused the Italian brand of breaching various written and verbal agreements to jointly develop a marketing initiative which he said Hong Kong-listed Prada unilaterally abandoned for accountability reasons.
Prada chairman Patrizio Bertelli, his fashion-designer wife Miuccia Prada and their son Lorenzo Bertelli, who serves as the firm’s executive director, were also named as defendants in the writ seen by the South China Morning Post on Friday.
Riss, whose real name is Jonathan Thierry Colin, is the founder of luxury fashion brand Jay Ahr and has gained a reputation for collaborating with international brands including Louis Vuitton, Hermes and Rolls-Royce.
The designer maintains a studio in an industrial building in Wong Chuk Hang in Hong Kong Island’s southern district. Ahrsenal Limited, the automotive arm of Jay Ahr, was named as the second plaintiff in the lawsuit.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said Riss was initially engaged by Patrizio Bertelli in February 2024 to transform Prada’s Galleria and Nylon bags, before the two parties agreed to work on a neo-prototype concept incorporating the signature elements of Prada and Jay Ahr.
The two sides eventually decided to work on an initiative later known as “Prada Strada”, which translates as “Prada Road”.
The plan was for Prada to “orchestrate immersive marketing and retail environments” by showcasing at least 10 Rolls-Royce Corniche cars redesigned by Riss in automotive exhibitions and rallies around the world.
Lawyers argued that Prada and its top executives had “actively and repeatedly encouraged” Riss to develop and commit to what could be a long-term strategic project no later than March last year, and the parties had signed a memorandum the following month setting out their intentions.
The memorandum reportedly stipulated the deadlines for Riss to submit his creations to Prada and the payment he would receive, including US$900,000 for each designed Rolls-Royce car.
Riss’s lawyers contended that although the parties had never entered into a formal contract, they had acted consistently as if a contract were already in place from June 2025.
They said Riss had invested significantly in technology, design and research for the project, including buying three Rolls-Royce Corniches at his own expense.
But Prada never finalised the paperwork, according to the court filing. In February this year, Lorenzo Bertelli reportedly told Riss through WhatsApp that the project had been “paused” for accountability reasons.
“This communication, made after more than two years of active collaboration, constituted a unilateral and wrongful repudiation by [Prada] of its obligations to the plaintiffs under the contract,” the writ said.
After being pressed by the designer’s lawyers for further explanations, Prada’s legal representatives denied the existence of any viable cause of action and allegedly characterised the collaboration as no more than “preliminary discussions”.
The fashion house’s legal team also allegedly threatened to seek legal costs for any claims initiated by the plaintiffs, while refusing to give any undertaking not to use or commercialise the “Prada Strada” concept without Riss’ involvement.
The plaintiffs are seeking at least US$5 million in damages from Prada, the Bertelli family or both, on grounds including breach of contract, restitution for work done and threatened copyright infringement.
They also asked the court to bar Prada from further developing the project on its own and to order Lorenzo Bertelli, who had previously given Riss a collection of Prada bags for redesign purposes, to pay him for the work done before reclaiming them.

data.title: Investor linked to Ningbo’s richest man buys Hong Kong luxury home for US$18.5m
data.description:
A buyer linked to the family behind Ningbo Tuopu Group has acquired a luxury villa in Hong Kong’s Tai Po area for HK$145.6 million (US$18.5 million), adding to signs of fresh mainland Chinese wealth making its way into the city’s high-end residential market.
Wu Xiaoming agreed to buy a home at Villa Lucca, 7 Lucca Avenue, on July 17 under an off-plan agreement for sale and purchase, Land Registry records showed.
The four-bedroom stand-alone garden house has a saleable area of 5,281 sq ft, implying a price of HK$27,571 per square foot.
Wu is a director of Mecca International Holding (Hong Kong), according to Companies Registry records.
The firm was previously headed by Wu Jianshu, chairman of Ningbo Tuopu Group, who was ranked 299th globally on the 2026 Hurun Global Rich List with a fortune of 77 billion yuan (US$11.4 billion), making him the richest man in Ningbo, in China’s eastern province of Zhejiang.
Wu Xiaoming was appointed a director of the Hong Kong company in 2018, replacing Wu Jianshu as the first-named director, records showed.
The transaction adds another link between Ningbo capital and Hong Kong property.
In June, a Ningbo government-backed innovation platform agreed to buy an office building in Wan Chai for HK$800 million, highlighting growing interest from the mainland city in Hong Kong property as prices remained well below their peaks.
Ningbo Tuopu Group, a major Chinese auto parts manufacturer headquartered in Ningbo and listed in Shanghai, submitted an application to the Hong Kong stock exchange to issue H shares and list on the main board, according to its filing in March.
The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Activity in Hong Kong’s luxury residential market has become more subdued. The Peak and Southern district recorded 12 sales in July, down 57 per cent from June, while the total value of transactions fell 48 per cent to about HK$2.35 billion, according to Midland Realty.
Transactions worth more than HK$100 million fell even more sharply – to four from 11 in June – while detached-house sales dropped to six from 11.
The month, however, produced several outsized deals, underscoring the resilience of the trophy-home segment.
A recent purchase at CK Asset’s luxury project 21 Borrett Road also shows that demand remains concentrated among high-end buyers. On August 4, a single buyer acquired two four-bedroom units on the 11th and 12th floors for nearly HK$300 million in total.
The developer said it had recently received more inquiries from buyers looking to purchase multiple units, with some attracted by the project’s privacy and layout.
The buyer in the latest deal bought adjoining units on consecutive floors, creating separate living spaces while allowing the family to live together, it added.
Midland Realty said on Wednesday that improved market sentiment after recent consolidation could encourage more owners to sell and widen their negotiating room, potentially drawing more buyers into the luxury segment.

data.title: Typhoon Dolphin: Hongkongers stuck in Okinawa prepare for low supplies, power cuts
data.description:
Hong Kong holidaymakers in Okinawa on Friday contended with depleted supermarket shelves, potential power cuts and violent weather as Typhoon Dolphin shut the Japanese island’s main airport and disrupted every direct flight home.
Social media images shared by Hong Kong-linked travel accounts showed empty bread shelves and torrential rain sweeping parts of the popular destination, although travellers said conditions varied significantly across the island.
Hong Kong travel account Papa Traveller said northern Okinawa, including the area around the Churaumi Aquarium, was experiencing “extremely heavy wind and rain”, while Naha in the south was temporarily caught in a gap between rainbands.

A Cantonese-language Okinawa page also posted a photograph of empty supermarket shelves and urged visitors, especially those staying in central and northern areas, to prepare candles and drinking water due to the possibility of electricity and water cuts.
But one traveller staying in Mihama observed calmer conditions, saying two major supermarkets still had sufficient supplies and there had been no panic buying.
Several major attractions and shopping centres, including DMM Kariyushi Aquarium and Aeon Mall Okinawa Rycom, were also closed on Friday because of the storm.
More than 500 flights were cancelled across southwestern Japan, and nearly 260,000 residents in Okinawa and Kagoshima prefectures were ordered to evacuate amid warnings of violent winds, heavy rain and high waves.

Naha International Airport closed on Friday, grounding all domestic and international flights, as Dolphin passed just north of Okinawa’s main island with maximum sustained winds of 144km/h (89.4mph).
All six Okinawa-bound flights scheduled to depart from Hong Kong on Friday were either cancelled or postponed, according to Hong Kong International Airport’s website.
HK Express cancelled flights 842, 844 and 824, while Hong Kong Airlines grounded 676 and 658.
Greater Bay Airlines flight 336D, originally scheduled to leave on Friday morning, was postponed until 5.15am on Monday.
All six flights scheduled to arrive in Hong Kong from Okinawa on Friday were also disrupted, with five cancelled and a Greater Bay Airlines service postponed until Monday.

Hong Kong’s Travel Industry Council said it estimated that there were only two to three tour groups in Okinawa, after communicating with major local tour agencies.
“All travellers are safe and are staying at their hotels for the time being,” executive director Fanny Yeung Shuk-fun said.
Steve Huen Kwok-chuen, executive director of EGL Tours, said his agency had two travel groups in Okinawa.
“The traffic has come to a standstill, and both tours have to stay in their hotels,” he said.
“All 35 travellers are safe and a tour group departing for Okinawa tomorrow has their flight delayed by a few hours, but all else is as per normal.”
Authorities in the prefecture said three men in their seventies suffered minor injuries, while about 240 people had sought shelter at evacuation centres across Okinawa by midday.

data.title: Tai Po inquiry sheds more light on final moments of firefighter Ho Wai-ho
data.description:
An independent inquiry into Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has released further details about the final moments of fallen firefighter Ho Wai-ho, who died in the line of duty while responding to the blaze at Wang Fuk Court last November.
An interim report from an interdepartmental fire investigation task force was released by the government-appointed independent committee on Thursday. The disclosure included images of Ho’s gear recovered from the scene.

“The post-fire visual inspection revealed that [Ho] might have been in prolonged contact with hot or burning objects, resulting in severe fire damage to his [uniform],” the report read.
The document noted that his PBI Matrix tunic and trousers, which were designed to withstand extreme temperatures for brief periods, were heavily compromised.
It was also noted that his anti-flash hood, which should be non-flammable, and his helmet showed little to no signs of unusual damage.
“No unusual damage was observed on [Ho’s] anti-flash hood and helmet, apart from a crack in the visor, which might have been caused by contact with a sharp or hard object either prior to or during the fire”, the document read.

Ho’s rubber boots might have also been in prolonged contact with hot or burning objects, the report pointed out.
“It is believed that the intense heat or flames exceeded the boots’ protective capacity over an extended period,” the document said.
Ho was among 168 people killed in the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November – Hong Kong’s deadliest blaze since 1948.

data.title: Beyond lithography: Chinese chip toolmaker achieves wafer polishing breakthrough
data.description:
Chinese chip-tool developers continue to make technical progress, with the latest breakthrough in wafer polishing – a critical manufacturing step that flattens and smooths silicon discs – even as the industry remains heavily dependent on foreign suppliers for more complex manufacturing procedures.
Hwatsing Technology, China’s leading producer of chemical mechanical polishing equipment, announced a new metrology system for six-inch wafers on Thursday. The ultra-precise measurement is designed to identify defects and ensure manufacturing consistency.
Wafers are thin, flat discs of semiconductor material that serve as the base for microchips, integrated circuits and electronic devices. Turning a raw wafer into a finished chip requires multiple steps, including coating the surface with photoresist, etching intricate layers and wiring microscopic transistors.
According to Hwatsing, its new measurement tool can be integrated directly into the polishing workflow – marking the country’s first six-inch metrology system paired with chemical mechanical polishing equipment. The set-up would enable real-time measurements before and after polishing, feeding live data back to the control system, the company said.
This direct integration could improve wafer uniformity and reduce waste, helping to address the inefficiencies of traditional production lines, it added.
Based in the northern city of Tianjin, Hwatsing reported that it had shipped the new system to an unnamed “leading domestic optical silicon materials producer”.
The system targets chips used in power devices, microelectromechanical systems and sensors, mostly with mature processing nodes. Such devices are widely used in electric vehicles, industrial equipment, consumer electronics and telecommunications infrastructure.
In terms of broader performance, domestic suppliers accounted for 21 per cent of China’s overall wafer-fabrication equipment market in 2025, while local wafer polishers enjoyed a higher rate of 39 per cent, according to a May report by brokerage Bernstein.
Hwatsing remained the “undisputed leader” in the domestic wafer polishing segment, supplying 85 per cent of the market, according to Bernstein. Across all competitors, Hwatsing’s share reached 37 per cent last year, up from 1 per cent in 2018, according to Chinese brokerage Soochow Securities.
However, the self-sufficiency rate for wafer metrology and inspection tools stood at just 10 per cent, despite domestic manufacturers recording a 63 per cent increase in revenue last year, it added.
Progress remains severely constrained in lithography – the strategic chipmaking technology dominated by Dutch giant ASML, which is barred from selling its most advanced deep-ultraviolet lithography systems and all-extreme-ultraviolet machines to China. According to Bernstein, there were “virtually no viable local alternatives” and “zero meaningful progress” in substituting the foreign technology.

data.title: Sugar for the pill: US$8b fund boosts Hong Kong’s biotech hub ambitions
data.description:
Hong Kong is stepping up its efforts to invest in a cluster of biotech companies, positioning itself as a linchpin in Beijing’s push to reach new levels of innovation and challenge the United States for dominance in the global pharmaceutical market.
Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), which manages about US$8 billion in assets and is wholly owned by the Hong Kong government, has built a biotech and healthcare technology investment portfolio covering both traditional Chinese and Western drugs to help transform the city into a global biotech hub.
“We have a pretty diversified portfolio covering upstream [to] downstream [of the full healthcare value chain], including Chinese medicine, Western medicine, [products] ranging from prevention, diagnostic treatments and [surgical] operations,” HKIC CEO Clara Chan Ka-chai said at the Global Health Summit in Hong Kong on Friday.
She added that HKIC has been linking AI and large language model firms with drug discovery companies in its portfolio, making the process of finding new medicines “cheaper, faster and better”.
HKIC has invested in more than 200 companies “covering high growth, high impact sectors, including biotech and health tech”, Chan said at the event, adding that the internal rate of return on the portfolio since its inception was 14 per cent as of end-2025.
The discussion among medical professionals and political leaders at the summit about Hong Kong’s role came as the rivalry between China and US in the pharmaceutical and life sciences sector has intensified. Washington has rolled out a series of measures including the Biosecure Act in December, targeting China’s biotech ambitions.
On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Commerce placed US DNA-authentication firm Applied DNA Sciences on a “countermeasures list”, accusing it of assisting US sanctions against Chinese companies over allegations of forced labour in western China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region.
China’s innovative drug development is closing the gap with the US, said Lu Shun, a medical professor at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, at the event.
China was the first country to complete research on a drug resistance problem that affects about 15 per cent of lung cancer patients with an EGFR gene mutation, Lu said. “The drug’s indication has currently only been approved in China and is about two years ahead of the US.”
“In the field of antibody-drug conjugates, we are basically at the same level as the United States,” he added.

Meanwhile, Ko Wing-man, director of New Frontier GBA Healthcare, said that Hong Kong acts as a bridge between mainland manufacturing scale and global capital markets.
The city can “combine leading basic research … with mainland [China’s] enormous manufacturing capability, engineering excellence, and rapidly expanding innovation capacity”, said Ko, also a member of the Standing Committee, National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.
Ko added that Hong Kong could serve as “the international gateway for China’s life science industry”.
HKIC healthcare investment focuses include liquid biopsies, female health, and longevity science, she said. HKIC has also invested in Hong Kong-grown embodied-AI and surgical-robotics companies.
The fund has attracted more than US$8 of long-term market and international capital for every US$1 invested, Chan said. About 70 per cent of its investment capital has been put in early and growth-stage companies.
As of Friday, 11 companies in HKIC’s portfolio have listed in Hong Kong, with 30 more either having submitted or in the process of submitting their applications for an initial public offering in the city this year.
A surge of technology-driven listings, including healthtech and pharmaceutical innovators, has spurred Hong Kong’s bourse to overhaul its listing framework, aiming to better accommodate high-growth enterprises seeking access to international capital. The exchange is in the process of advancing reforms that would permit confidential filings and lower the market capitalisation threshold for eligible issuers.

data.title: HKU virologist spared conviction for assaulting man and damaging his phone
data.description:
A University of Hong Kong (HKU) virologist has been spared a criminal conviction for assaulting a man and damaging his mobile phone at a railway station last year.
Eastern Court on Friday placed Vijaykrishna Dhanasekaran on a two-year bind-over order and instructed him to pay HK$800 (US$102) in damages, after he admitted attacking a stranger at Hong Kong MTR station on August 17, 2025.
The 48-year-old associate professor, who heads the university’s pathogen evolution lab, could be fined HK$2,000 if he failed to keep the peace during the bind-over period.
The court heard Dhanasekaran was involved in a “trivial dispute” with retiree Raimundo Kwok Chun-tung, 56, inside a lift connecting to the Airport Express shortly after 6pm.
Dhanasekaran used his mobile phone to film Kwok, who then used his phone to film the defendant in return.
In the heat of the moment, the defendant knocked Kwok’s Samsung Galaxy Note 20 to the ground, then pushed him several times and kicked the HK$3,000 phone out of the lift.
A civil servant who witnessed the incident called police. Dhanasekaran remained silent under caution.
Kwok sustained scratches to his left arm and cuts to his left knee, while reporting mild pain in his right hip. He spent HK$800 to repair the cracked screen and dents on his phone.
Prosecutors agreed to drop charges of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and criminal damage on the condition that the defendant accept the bind-over order.
Dhanasekaran joined HKU’s School of Public Health in 2020 while also holding research positions in Singapore and Australia, according to the university’s website. He was credited for his study on the worldwide resurgence of the deadly H5N1, the virus that causes bird flu.

data.title: Missing man, 58, found dead in Ma On Shan after days-long search effort
data.description:
Hong Kong police have found the body of a missing 58-year-old man in Ma On Shan, with his cause of death to be confirmed following an autopsy.
Officers received a report at around 12.50am on Friday from a passer-by who had spotted a man lying on the ground near a slope on Nui Po Shan in Ma On Shan.
Upon arrival at the scene, officers confirmed the death of the man, who was believed to be the missing person last seen at King Lam Estate in Tseung Kwan O on the afternoon of July 24.

The force received a report on the same day from the family of a man surnamed Chan, stating that they had lost contact with him.
A police spokeswoman said the man was suspected to have become lost.
Police, the Fire Services Department, the Government Flying Service and the Civil Aid Service had mounted a joint search and rescue operation for days before finding him.

data.title: China’s Kimi K3 AI model escapes a closed cyber test: researchers
data.description:
China’s top open-weight AI model Kimi K3 broke out of its isolated test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation, according to US security researchers, following similar high-profile incidents involving closed frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic that highlight the growing challenge of constraining AI behaviour.
Kimi K3, released last month by Beijing-based Moonshot AI, escaped from a supposedly isolated sandbox environment, accessed the open internet, and found solutions on the developer platform GitHub, US firm Frontier Security said in a blog post on Thursday.
The incident occurred when the firm tested Kimi K3’s defensive cybersecurity capabilities using a benchmark evaluation from the AI Security Institute – a UK government research organisation, according to Frontier Security researchers Paul Kassianik and Yaron Singer.
A “basic network misconfiguration” in the benchmark framework allowed Kimi K3 to flee its digital testing cage and look up answers on the internet, effectively cheating the test, they said.
Kimi K3’s escape, however, did not involve the hacking of an external system, unlike recent breaches caused by OpenAI and Anthropic models.

Last month, OpenAI said its flagship GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased, “even more capable” system broke out of a sandboxed environment and hacked the open-source developer platform Hugging Face to obtain secret information containing answers to an internal test.
Anthropic later disclosed that it had also identified three previous incidents where its Claude models – including Opus 4.7, Mythos 5 and an internal research model – breached the infrastructure of three undisclosed organisations.
Even without a direct hack, the Kimi K3 incident could still be “potentially more harmful” because of the model’s open-weight nature, which makes it publicly available to adversarial actors, Frontier Security said.
Kimi K3’s ability to circumvent its test parameters also reflected the model’s weaker internal safeguards, according to one of the researchers.
“It found the misconfiguration itself, by probing its own network settings,” Kassianik wrote on social media platform X on Friday. “Most publicly available frontier models have internal guardrails that stop them. K3 didn’t blink.”
Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
The rapidly advancing capabilities of frontier AI have heightened global cybersecurity concerns, pushing the role of widely accessible open-weight models to the centre of an escalating debate.
While critics warn that advanced open-weight models lower technical barriers for malicious actors, several US AI leaders have defended open-source systems’ key role in cyber defence.
American tech giants including Nvidia, Palantir and Meta Platforms last month signed an open letter urging Washington not to restrict open-weight models. While open models carried real risks, they also enabled cybersecurity defenders to detect and respond to emerging threats posed by AI-equipped attackers, the companies argued.
That point was underscored when Hugging Face had to rely on GLM-5.2, an open-weight model from Beijing-based Zhipu AI, to contain the OpenAI attack after major proprietary US models refused to process the security logs due to safety guardrails.

data.title: Hang Lung Properties names former Starbucks China head Leo Tsoi as new CEO
data.description:
Hong Kong developer Hang Lung Properties has tapped Leo Tsoi Tak Lun, CEO of Toys ‘R’ Us Asia and former head of Starbucks China, as its new CEO and executive director.
Tsoi will join Hang Lung Group and Hang Lung Properties on September 7 as CEO-designate and executive director ahead of formally assuming the CEO role on October 1. He succeeds Weber Lo Wai-pak, who retires on August 31 after serving as CEO for eight years, the developer said in a statement on Friday.
Tsoi’s appointment marks Hang Lung’s first CEO change since Adriel Chan took over from his father Ronnie Chan as chairman in 2024, in the latest leadership shift at the family-controlled property group.
Tsoi, 56, has more than three decades of experience in retail and business management in Asia. He currently serves as CEO of Toys ‘R’ Us Asia, where he expanded the brand’s appeal to the “kidult” segment, and revived business growth across Greater China and Southeast Asia, according to Hang Lung.

Prior to this role, he headed Starbucks China as CEO after holding several senior leadership positions in the US coffee giant. Earlier in his career, Tsoi “built a strong leadership foundation” at PepsiCo and Procter & Gamble Greater China, Hang Lung said.
“As I step into this role, I look forward to partnering with our talented team to strengthen relationships with stakeholders, tenants, and customers,” Tsoi said in a statement. “I am grateful to Adriel and the boards for their trust, and to Weber for laying down such a strong foundation to build upon.”
The developer announced the management shift in its half-year earnings released on July 31, noting that a CEO-designate had been appointed without naming them.
Chairman Adriel Chan said Tsoi’s track record of “driving growth through excellence” made him the best candidate to “lead Hang Lung into the next chapter”.
At a press conference announcing the group’s earnings, Chan credited Lo with leading the company through “challenging” years, which included the Covid-19 pandemic and China’s prolonged property downturn.
Hang Lung announced the retirement of Lo in December.
Additional reporting by Peggy Ye
